It addresses suffering *now* but doesn't change the underlying vulnerability. In contrast, $100 directed to research has a different character: it funds the kind of work — surveillance systems, vaccine platforms, epidemiological modeling, early-warning infrastructure — whose benefits compound over time and across populations. A marginal dollar in research can shift a threshold that matters for millions of future people.

There's also a category-of-risk argument: pandemics are low-probability but high-consequence events that markets systematically under-prepare for. Flood relief, by contrast, tends to attract substantial attention and funding in the immediate aftermath. The marginal philanthropic dollar is, in my view, more valuable where it's hardest to get — preventive research for rare-but-catastrophic risks.
